program_overview.title: C++ for Kids
program_overview.tagline: A serious language, taught at a child's pace, with a game or puzzle at the end of every lesson.
program_overview.description:
C++ has a reputation for being hard, and for adults learning alone it can be. For a 9 to 12-year-old with a patient teacher, it is something else: a language that makes the computer's thinking visible. Every variable has a type, every line ends with a semicolon, and the compiler says exactly what it did not understand. Children who learn this way pick up habits of precision that make every later language easier.

This 6-month live course is written for that age. It starts with what a program is and what a compiler does, then builds one idea at a time: printing and input, variables and arithmetic, decisions with if and else, loops, functions, lists with vectors, strings and finally grouping data with structs. Each idea arrives inside something a child wants to make, such as a times-table trainer, a number guessing game, a secret code machine, a pet simulator, tic-tac-toe or a maze. Topics that need more maturity, like pointers and memory management, are left for our C++ for Teens course.

The final month introduces the kind of short puzzle problems used in programming contests. USACO, the USA Computing Olympiad, accepts C++ solutions and starts every new participant in its Bronze division, so students finish with a clear picture of what that next step looks like if they enjoy it. Classes are live and small enough for the teacher to read every child's code, and every month ends with a short check so parents can see real progress.
what_makes_this_different: Written for ages 9 to 12: one new idea at a time, explained with pictures and everyday examples before any syntax
A game or puzzle in every lesson, so practice feels like play while the habits stay rigorous
Compiler errors taught as clues, not failures: children learn to read them and fix their own code
Pointers and manual memory left for later on purpose, so younger students build confidence before complexity
A first taste of contest-style problem solving in the final month, with USACO Bronze as a visible next step
A clear bridge to our C++ for Teens course for students who want to keep going

learning_path.phase_3: Games and puzzles: random numbers, grids and nested loops, contest-style problems and a capstone project

career_outcomes: Confident C++ basics: variables, conditions, loops, functions, vectors, strings and structs
The ability to read compiler errors and debug their own programs
A folder of finished games and tools they wrote themselves
A strong base for C++ for Teens, Python, or contest programming later

phase_1_first_programs.title: PHASE 1: First Programs (Months 1-2, Weeks 1-8)
phase_1_first_programs.description: From what a program is to loops that draw patterns and run games. Every concept is shown on paper first, then typed, run and changed.

week_1_2.title: Weeks 1-2: What Code Is and Your First Program
topics: What a program is: instructions a computer follows exactly
What a compiler does, explained as a translator
The shape of a C++ program: include, main, braces and semicolons
Printing words and numbers with cout
Comments as notes to your future self
Reading a compiler error and finding the line it points to
projects: Name banner: a program that prints a decorated banner with the student's name and favourite things
week_1_2.practice: Write three short programs that print a joke, a poem and a box drawn with symbols

week_3_4.title: Weeks 3-4: Variables, Input and Arithmetic
topics: Variables as labelled boxes, and the types int, double, char and string
Reading input with cin
Plus, minus, times and divide in code
Why 7 / 2 gives 3 with whole numbers, and what % does
Updating a variable: score = score + 10 and the shortcut +=
Choosing clear variable names
projects: Pocket calculator and age-in-days converter that ask the user for numbers and print answers
week_3_4.practice: Build a pizza-sharing program that works out slices each and slices left over using / and %
week_3_4.assessment: Month 1 check: write a short input and arithmetic program from a plain-English description

week_5_6.title: Weeks 5-6: If, Else and Making Choices
topics: Comparing values with ==, !=, <, >, <= and >=
if, else if and else
Combining conditions with and, or and not
The classic mistake of = instead of ==
Tracing a program by hand with a table
Planning decisions with a simple flowchart
projects: Quiz show: a five-question quiz that keeps score and gives a message based on the result
week_5_6.practice: Write a rock, paper, scissors judge that decides the winner from two typed choices

week_7_8.title: Weeks 7-8: Loops That Repeat
topics: while loops and the idea of repeating until something changes
for loops for counting
Loop counters, totals and running scores
Avoiding loops that never end
Drawing star patterns and triangles with loops
break and continue, used sparingly
projects: Times-table trainer and a number guessing game that says higher or lower until the player wins
week_7_8.practice: Print the 1 to 12 times tables neatly, then a staircase of stars of any height the user chooses
week_7_8.assessment: Phase 1 assessment: a loop and decision program built in class, plus a short explanation of how it works

phase_2_building_blocks.title: PHASE 2: Building Blocks (Months 3-4, Weeks 9-16)
phase_2_building_blocks.description: The tools that let programs grow without getting messy: functions, lists, text and grouped data, each taught inside a small game or tool.

week_9_10.title: Weeks 9-10: Functions
topics: Why we split programs into functions
Writing a function, calling it and passing values in
Returning an answer from a function
void functions that just do something
Local variables and why they stay inside their function
Testing a function with a few known answers
projects: Shape helper: functions that draw squares and triangles and work out area and perimeter
week_9_10.practice: Rewrite the quiz show from month 2 so each question is one function call

week_11_12.title: Weeks 11-12: Lists with Vectors
topics: Storing many values in a vector
Adding items with push_back and reading them by position
Looping over a vector to total, count and find the biggest
Positions start at zero, and what happens past the end
Sorting a list with sort
Choosing between a single variable and a list
projects: High score board: enter scores, sort them and print the top five with medals beside them
week_11_12.practice: Store a week of temperatures and print the warmest day, the coldest day and the average
week_11_12.assessment: Month 3 check: a function and vector task solved from a written problem

week_13_14.title: Weeks 13-14: Working with Text
topics: Strings as lists of characters
Length, indexing and looping through a string
Changing letters to upper or lower case
Characters as numbers underneath
Counting vowels, reversing words and checking palindromes
Reading a full line of text with getline
projects: Secret code machine: a shift cipher that encodes and decodes messages between friends
week_13_14.practice: Write a word game that tells the player how many letters their guess shares with a secret word

week_15_16.title: Weeks 15-16: Grouping Data with Structs
topics: Why related values belong together
Defining a struct with fields such as name, hunger and happiness
Creating and changing struct values
A vector of structs for a class list or a team
Passing a struct to a function
Designing data before writing code
projects: Virtual pet: a pet that gets hungry and bored over time and responds to feeding and play commands
week_15_16.practice: Extend the pet so the player can look after three pets stored in one vector
week_15_16.assessment: Phase 2 assessment: a small program that uses functions, a vector and a struct together

phase_3_games_and_puzzles.title: PHASE 3: Games and Puzzles (Months 5-6, Weeks 17-24)
phase_3_games_and_puzzles.description: Everything comes together in bigger text games, grid puzzles and the short problem-solving tasks used in programming contests, ending with a capstone each child designs.

week_17_18.title: Weeks 17-18: Random Numbers and a Text Adventure
topics: Making random numbers for dice, cards and surprises
Planning a game as rooms, choices and items
A game loop that runs until the player wins or quits
Keeping track of health, gold and inventory
Splitting a bigger program into many small functions
Testing every path through the game
projects: Dungeon adventure: a text adventure with rooms, random encounters, an inventory and a win condition
week_17_18.practice: Add two new rooms and one new item, then ask someone at home to play it

week_19_20.title: Weeks 19-20: Grids and Nested Loops
topics: A grid as a vector of vectors
Nested loops to print and search a grid
Rows, columns and checking neighbours
Checking for three in a row
Moving a player around a maze with letters
Keeping a grid game fair and bug-free
projects: Tic-tac-toe for two players and a maze game where the player finds the exit
week_19_20.practice: Add a move counter to the maze and a replay option to tic-tac-toe
week_19_20.assessment: Month 5 check: a grid task built from a short written specification

month_6_puzzles_and_capstone.title: Month 6: Contest Puzzles and the Capstone

week_21_22.title: Weeks 21-22: Thinking Like a Problem Solver
topics: Reading a puzzle problem: input, output and the example cases
Working out the answer by hand before coding
Patterns that keep coming up: counting, finding the largest, simulating step by step
Testing with small cases and tricky edge cases
What USACO is and how its Bronze division works
Staying calm when the first idea does not work
projects: Puzzle notebook: eight short contest-style problems solved, each with a sentence on the idea behind it
week_21_22.practice: Solve two puzzle problems a week and write down one mistake and how you found it

week_23_24.title: Weeks 23-24: Capstone Project and Showcase
topics: Choosing a project idea that fits two weeks
Planning the data, the functions and the game loop
Building in small steps and testing as you go
Asking for feedback and improving the project
Presenting the program and explaining one clever part
Next steps: C++ for Teens, Python or contest practice
projects: Capstone: an original game or tool planned, built and presented by the student
week_23_24.practice: Write a short guide that explains how to play or use the capstone project
week_23_24.assessment: Final assessment: the capstone project, a short code walkthrough and a set of small coding tasks covering the whole course

faqs.question: Is C++ too hard for a 9 or 10-year-old?
faqs.answer: Not when it is taught at the right pace. Children cope well with C++ when each idea is introduced on its own, shown on paper first, and practised inside a small game. We leave the genuinely hard parts, such as pointers and manual memory management, for our C++ for Teens course, so younger students build confidence before complexity.

faqs.question: Should my child learn Python or C++ first?
faqs.answer: Both are good first languages. Python gets results faster with less punctuation. C++ asks for more precision, such as types and semicolons, and children who learn it early tend to be careful, systematic coders. If your child enjoys puzzles and detail, or is interested in programming contests later, C++ is a strong choice. The free demo is a good place to see which suits them.

faqs.question: Does my child need to know Scratch first?
faqs.answer: No. The course starts from what a program is. Children who have used Scratch often recognise loops and conditions quickly, but complete beginners do just as well with a little extra practice in the first month.

faqs.question: What will my child build?
faqs.answer: A quiz show, a number guessing game, a times-table trainer, a high score board, a secret code machine, a virtual pet, a text adventure, tic-tac-toe, a maze game and an original capstone project, plus a notebook of solved puzzle problems.

faqs.question: What software do we need?
faqs.answer: Only a laptop or desktop with a browser and a stable internet connection. We begin with a free online C++ compiler so nothing needs installing. Later in the course we can help set up a free compiler on the computer if the family wants one.

faqs.question: Does this prepare my child for USACO?
faqs.answer: It prepares them to start. USACO accepts C++ solutions and every new participant begins in the Bronze division. The final month introduces the kind of short problems used there and explains how the contest works. Moving up the divisions takes much more practice, which our contest programming courses cover for older students.

faqs.question: How is this different from C++ for Teens?
faqs.answer: C++ for Teens is a longer course for ages 13 to 18 that goes into pointers, object-oriented programming, the standard library, data structures and games with graphics. This course is for ages 9 to 12 and covers the foundations slowly and thoroughly, so a child who finishes it is well prepared to join the teen course later.

faqs.question: How are the classes run?
faqs.answer: Live online classes, twice a week, with a real teacher, in a group of 15 to 20 students, a mini batch of up to 6, or one to one. Current fees for your region are shown in the pricing section of this page.

faqs.question: Can we try a class first?
faqs.answer: Yes. Book a free demo class. The teacher writes and runs a small C++ program with your child, sees how they think, and suggests whether group, mini batch or one-to-one classes fit best. There is no obligation to enrol.
